enabling promotion of paraxial beam quality and correction of spherical 
aberration simultaneously.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics is insufficient in gauging a model's encoding capabilities and stresses the importance of incorporating a task-specific evaluation approach. To facilitate such assessment, the researchers introduce a comprehensive suite of tools for preprocessing, experimentation, and analysis of encoder models in dialogue contexts. As an alternative to standard text generation evaluation, they propose using a dialogue classification task as a proxy for measuring the quality of underlying representations. Specifically, they investigate the model's ability to predict a user's sentiment towards the agent in the following utterance. Their experiments reveal that prominent generative models, such as GPT-2, fall short in capturing high-quality encoder representations for dialogue tasks. Furthermore, they advocate for the inclusion of such analysis during the development stage of dialogue models to ensure their latent representations are suitable for underlying encoding tasks. All experiment results and tools used in this work are openly available online at https://github.com/RepsLab/evaluating-dialo-gen.

Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in urban environments by leveraging local descriptor matching.  However, matching local descriptors remains a computationally challenging task due to the large size of feature vectors and the scale of description databases required for global place recognition in urban settings.  In order to overcome these limitations, this research proposes a innovative approach that leverages a deep learning network to perform place recognition directly from raw LiDAR data at a reduced input dimension.  Our method transforms a local view of the surroundings into a compact compact vector, which is then compared to stored descriptors to identify matching places.  Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves a balance of accuracy and processing speed, generating a matching descriptor database five times smaller than conventional methods, while still delivering acceptable accuracy in real-world urban environments.  Furthermore, this technique can be applied to real-time global place recognition systems for autonomous vehicles and drones.

Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different machine types and utilizes a large scale cloud benchmark to compare their real-world streaming capabilities. The results provide a foundation for developing efficient strategies for leveraging cloud resources in video streaming and oﬀering more performant streaming experiences at a lower cost. As cloud utilization for video streaming grows, transparent delivery of high-quality content to viewers will be paramount. To achieve this, we also assess the impact of video streaming applications on Virtual Machine performance and found that low-load sharing has negligible impact, whereas high-load sharing can lead to noticeable performance degradation. This study is the first to empirically investigate how video transcoding and streaming affect each other when run on cloud resources.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic static structure factor of massless Dirac systems to derive key properties. This derivation基于量子电子气体在二维系统的高精度数值模拟。Lattice size 1000$\times$1000 上的 MPRG 算法被用来计算结构因子，以低温度下无质量 Dirac 系统的比热容量线性关系 $C_v \propto T$ 的线性比例常数。利用结构因子的第一矩和二矩来计算这一线性比例常数。我们发现这一常数与线性散热的预测一致，而之前的数值计算结果与线性关系偏离。此外，我们比较了无质量 Dirac 系统的结构因子与连续空间中的结构因子，并发现它们在深层紫外区域是一致的。

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study.

We investigated a cyclic universe containing holographic dark energy with different infrared cutoffs, excluding the Big Rip singularity. The study reveals that, in the absence of interaction between the cosmos sectors, the HDE model using the Hubble radius cutoff behaves like a cosmological constant within cyclic cosmology. Furthermore, we discovered that cyclic patterns of contraction and expansion may occur for both interacting and non-interacting universes, provided that the Granda-Oliveros cutoff is slightly larger than 1/l. However, this scenario is unstable due to the gradual increase in the cosmos' total energy across successive cycles. When considering an entropy-based approach, our results suggest that if interaction exists, the universe's entropy remains unaffected by cycling, but complete interaction leads to an infinite entropy growth, contradicting the second law of thermodynamics.

Gnutzmann and Smilansky previously developed a formula for the bond scattering matrix of a graph using a Hermitian matrix. This formula was expressed as an average of the trace of the fourth power of a unitary matrix whose elements followed a Gaussian distribution. We refine this formula by generalizing it to ensembles of Hermitian and unitary matrices from the CUE(r), SU(N)/SU(N)xSU(N), and various GOE(c) families, parameterized by their underlying probability distributions. Additionally, we provide new expressions for the moments of a product of diagonal matrices with entries drawn from specific distributions, including Bessel and Hermite ensembles, and explore possible applications of our findings.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G.

In experiments involving the Belle II particle accelerator, we can gather significant information about possible axion-like particles through specific decay processes involving B mesons. These processes, such as the decay of a B meson into a B bar and two photons mediated by a possible axion-like particle, provide an opportunity to study the properties of these particles. By analyzing data from the Belle II experiment, we can estimate the frequency of certain decay processes, such as the decay of a B meson into a B bar and two photons, and use this information to set limits on the properties of axion-like particles. Our calculations show that the Belle II experiment can determine the frequency of certain decay processes with a certain level of precision within nine years, and this level of precision is sufficient to study the properties of axion-like particles with certain mass ranges. By examining the relationship between the mass and the phi meson of axion-like particles, we can study the possible existence of these particles within certain mass ranges.

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized to reveal the
roots of this issue and suggest that pre-trained contextual language models'
diachronic assessment may be constrained by their training data. We further
propose that our novel approach can mitigate the discrepancies between the
these models' understanding of language and real-world usage.

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) containing active black holes at the heart of the galaxy allow for investigating the mass and spin of black holes through their spectral analysis. A theoretical model is used to analyze the electromagnetic spectrum of a T-type blazar, J1638+418, also known as Evil Eye, which has a very active black hole with an unusual spectrum. A standard seven-parameter model successfully replicates a similar spectrum previously created for this AGN. Based on this model, a minimum black hole mass of 1.4 times the solar mass is inferred, assuming an accretion disk with no thickness. If the disk has a thickness, the minimum mass increases to 2.2 times the solar mass. Furthermore, a black hole spin of at least 0.2 is required to produce the observed X-ray spectrum. Evolutionary simulations of the AGN reveal a decrease in the black hole's mass and a corresponding decrease in various electromagnetic wavebands' emissions.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed light-sheet
fluorescence imaging to capture the movement of cell nuclei in the developing mouse
cerebellum. Our observations reveal the precise rates at which nuclei migrate both
vertically and horizontally. We detect the occurrence of dividing cells within the
neuroepithelial layer and associated movements of the cell nucleus. Our results show
that lengthening of the cell cycle correlates with an increase in the radius of cell
division within the cerebellum. Furthermore, our data indicate that during S-phase,
cells expand in length along the axis perpendicular to the ventricular surface in the
expanding mouse cerebellum.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions.

Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as their primary means of communication. Due to their accessibility and private data storage, these emails are vulnerable to cyber threats and can serve as lucrative targets. Our proposed approach aims to examine research institutions' internal communication networks for potential security breaches. Initially, we gathered and analyzed email data from multiple research institutions, incorporating their email headers, attachment names, and calendar information. A stochastic model was then developed to simulate the spread of access to these networks. Our research identified significant vulnerabilities within these networks - specifically, we found that approximately 9% of nodes were vulnerable to security breaches, with the U of T showing the lowest risk at 2.5%. Our results also revealed that around 85% of nodes within these networks were not directly accessible to attackers. Furthermore, we discovered that the distribution of nodes with multiple connections conformed to a geometric distribution, characterized by a parameter of 0.875. Due to the sensitive nature of our gathering process, detailed data cannot be disclosed; however, our findings can be utilized for the purpose of identifying risks inherent in email-based communication systems within research institutions.

Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that numerous cuprates may be positioned near such a singularity, 
and propose, in conjunction with the resonating valence bond theory, that 
the proximity to this singularity could be pivotal in triggering a drive for 
antiferromagnetism and the emergence of the pseudogap.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 600 meters of rock above it. The apparatus consists of six layers of plastic-scintillator detectors that identify these muons. It also includes a high-sensitivity low-background detector in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory and a precise time-correlation system. This system is designed to accurately measure the position and movement of muons relative to the detector in the laboratory, thus enabling identification of associated spallation neutrons. Furthermore, this apparatus enables investigation of several key issues in several areas, including the distribution of high-energy cosmic rays at the Earth's surface, the production of spallation neutrons, and the neutron flux at the laboratory site.

Ground-based observations of planetary systems are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Nonetheless, many exoplanets still remain unconfirmed due to the lack of sufficient data compared to our solar system. Planetary candidates identified by TESS often require extensive ground-based observations, especially radial velocity (RV) measurements for multiple seasons, to validate their status. If RV measurements are not available for some of these planet candidates, transiting large amplitude signals could still be investigated by performing RV residual analysis after removing the impact of the known bodies in the system's frequency domain. This method could potentially yield additional insights into the system's dynamics and even yield discoveries of new exoplanets without relying solely on RV data. As a proof of concept, we utilized TESS's open data to analyze a representative sample of systems with high RV signal-to-noise ratios in order to compare their transit profiles with those of their validated counterparts in terms of the impact of the low-frequency components of their RVs. This study demonstrates the feasibility of using frequency domain data to analyze the systems with insufficient RV data for validation, including the possibility of using TESS's TDCS to identify such systems for further follow-up with radial velocity measurements which could lead to full validation of the system.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately, prompting the need for a more efficient method of verifying ID cards.  To address this, a modified version of the CRNN model was employed to automatically verify ID cards by converting their visual images into text.  Specifically, two different convolutional neural architectures and optimization techniques were experimented with to enhance accuracy.  Furthermore, an attention mechanism was integrated into the model to improve its performance by focusing on key features.  Moreover, an external memory component was incorporated into the model to expand its capacity for correcting and storing text.  Test results show that this enhanced model outperformed its predecessor with an accuracy rate of 99.4 percent.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. To understand how the YORP effect influences a given asteroid's rotation, it's essential to consider both its shape and thermal properties. Taking the case of 2867 Steins as an example, researchers used light curve analysis to obtain its spin period, orientation, rotation rate, and axis of rotation. Additionally, they obtained its surface dielectric properties and used existing models to simulate its interior temperature distribution. By combining observational and modeling data, they derived a quantitative expression of the YORP acceleration acceleration_yorp = 5.66e-14 m/s^2 * \epsilon_0(1.06 - 0.06 k), which can be employed to analyze the YORP effect's impact on the asteroid's rotational dynamics and its potential companion, orchard.

The Facebook's MIWS dataset is an innovative resource for analyzing transcripts of group events, which is being used to explore how topics are developed within online communities. Our initial examination of this dataset involved conducting content analysis to identify key characteristics of certain topics. Notably, we discovered that discussions on polarizing issues elicit higher levels of interaction from users than discussions on other issues. This phenomenon is manifested in multiple ways - participants who express disagreeable opinions are met with greater encouragement from their peers, their opinions are more frequently targeted in critiques, their posts are more likely to go viral, and their profile information is examined more closely by others. These dynamics have significant implications for the design of social networking platforms.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

Precise stellar characteristics are crucial for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. A new approach has been developed for determining these properties using spectral data. This approach utilizes age to derive fundamental stellar parameters and a 'reduced spectrum' to refine the estimates of temperature and surface gravity while correcting for binary systems or exoplanets. A comprehensive database of M-dwarf star parameters, including 630 systems, has been compiled based on this approach. The database's reliability is demonstrated through an exercise where the database's parameters are compared with previously estimated values, showcasing a significant improvement in accuracy and consistency among the stars with available parallax measurements. The approach's robustness is highlighted by an example where a suspected binary system, Gl 581, was analyzed and found to be consistent with being a single star.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed waves passing through interfaces and line waves that exist when both interfaces are connected.
However, a key characteristic of modes in these scenarios is their inability to propagate significant energy in reverse.
This limitation can be overcome by implementing two separate interfaces that have mirror symmetry properties and are disconnected from each other.
In this study, many types of geometries and symmetry breaking methods were considered, resulting in the line waves that can have significant reverse transmissibility.
It has been shown that these modes can be carefully designed to operate over a wide range of frequencies due to their dual symmetry nature.
Furthermore, a practical application demonstrated in this research involves a 35 GHz frequency band sensing application.

Although a key function in database management, query evaluation classification lacks comprehensive guidelines when dealing with self-joined queries. Our investigation aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how self-joins impact the complexity of enumerating database results, building on existing research. By extending two known categories of classification to incorporate self-joined queries with respect to efficiency, this study provides an in-depth analysis and illustrates potential enumeration strategies using self-joins. These advancements lead to more complex subcases with increased enumeration difficulty. Additionally, this study introduces an existing subcase that allows for more straightforward enumeration.

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, not all functions defined by these types of transducers are guaranteed to be computable. In contrast, functions defined by deterministic transducers are always continuous, but many non-deterministic transducers-defined functions remain non-computable. This work extends this understanding by defining and characterizing a broader class - 'regular' functions - encompassing both deterministic and non-deterministic types, using a combined logical and computational approach.

Researchers have analyzed collision data with an integrated luminosity of 3 inverse femtobarns, and through amplitude analysis of specific two-body decay events, have discovered that the $B^0$ decay to a pair of $K^*$ mesons exhibits a higher fraction of longitudinal polarization than the $B^0_s$ decay to the same mesons. Furthermore, this difference in longitudinal polarization was utilized to determine the branching fraction of the $B^0$ decay to a pair of $K^*$ mesons.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems. Although effective for simple applications with traditional reservoir computing, the method struggles with highly complex time series data due to large amounts of required training data. A new variation of reservoir computing has been developed that utilizes reservoir expansion. This new variation achieves high accuracy even with minimal training data for complex systems. It has been successfully applied to model atmospheric conditions on the Jupiter moon and to forecast future atmospheric conditions, outperforming a standard reservoir computing approach.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons have become a dominant tool for generating signals across multiple domains, particularly in terms of efficiency and flexibility. Furthermore flexibility has been shown to be increased with the use of global fixation modules in signal representations that encompass both time and frequency dimensions. This study proposes two key enhancements to this architecture: 1) mixing strategies have been developed that lead to significant improvements in performance for complex video restoration tasks by leveraging both local and global features more effectively than alternative methods, 2) impressive performance gains in efficient multi-domain super-resolution that leads to notable improvements over existing ENR schemes with only minimal increase in computational costs leading to significant recovery of high-frequency details at both super-resolved and intermediate stages of the process.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Although research has identified multiple dimensions of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy, conflicting studies have produced varied results. To resolve this discrepancy, a new dataset was created using the GPTJ language model to present a large sample of stimuli spanning a continuum from inanimate objects to living animals and humans. Using both decode and encoding models, a seven-dimensional space was developed, with two key hypotheses proposed: (1) the ventral temporal cortex processes animacy through a hierarchical system where parts are evaluated within a whole context, and (2) animacy representation is influenced by ecological factors such as visual complexity and salience. Furthermore, neural pattern decodes were used to test two theories: the compositional hypothesis and the ecological hypothesis. Results indicated a preference for the ecological hypothesis over the compositional hypothesis.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases can be attributed in part to super-spreader events.  
These rare occurrences allow an epidemic to spread rapidly, masking the typical value of the super-spreader exponent $\tau$ which is greater than $3$.  
We propose a method to estimate $\tau$ by analyzing a log-percolation process.  
This approach can be applied to a wide range of models, including those with multi-type agents, time-varying transmission rates, and SP-virus models.  
Our results show that in a large population, the average number of infected super-spreaders increases as a power of the number of infected regular agents.  
Based on this, we argue that using a single value for $R_0$ in super-spreader epidemics is misleading.  
To address this limitation, we suggest using a time-varying $R_0(t)$ instead.  
In our model, we incorporate $\tau$ into a time-dependent function for $R_0(t)$.  
As a case study, we apply this framework to the COVID-19 epidemic in South Korea.  
Here, we model government interventions as changes in time, and show that our $\tau$ value of approximately $3.2$ fits the data well.  
Moreover, our model fits both the total number of cases and the distribution of super-spreader events observed in South Korea.

Let K be a fixed closed subspaces of K. An operator T on K is said to be codiskcyclic if there exists a subscyclic vector for the pair (T,K). 

Let sigma (D) denote the discrete set of points in the complex plane. A point lambda in sigma (d) is called an eigenvalue of an operator D if the corresponding eigenspace is nontrivial. 

In this paper we show that a normal operator N is codiskcyclic if and only if it has countably many distinct eigenvalues. 

We also provide conditions for the direct sum of countably many normal operators to be codiskcyclic.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously but its complex sources required further investigation. A comprehensive analysis of various factors contributing to Bperp bias has been conducted, including uncertainties in line-of-sight magnetic field, vector magnetogram calibration, contrast and correlation length of magnetic field patterns, and inversion algorithms. To quantify the effect, a first-order formula has been developed, which is based on the local correlation length and contrast of magnetograms. This formula is found to be broadly applicable regardless of specific assumptions about the magnetogram patterns. Comparing this formula to numerical simulations and actual observations from the Sun confirms its effectiveness. The resulting bias typically exceeds pixel noise in SDO/IPS data and can result in an overestimation of the non-potentiality of magnetic fields by a factor of two or more. The study highlights the critical role of filling factors in determining bipolar free energy. Additionally, modifications to data and implications for solar physics research are discussed. A code incorporated into the DSDP package is proposed as a useful tool for processing SDO/ADIT data.

A new set of infrared images has been created using the Webb Telescope to study the NGC 3603 star formation region. Using these images, researchers were able to obtain updated visuals of young star clusters by removing contamination from surrounding sources. When analyzing the main sequence of the Infrared Photometric Distribution, distinct groupings can be seen at 3, 5, and 8 microns that correspond to different population segments. A passing comparison was made between the clusters' colors and those predicted by theoretical models. Additionally, the study revealed several features not previously seen with visible images, offering valuable color information for specific stellar groups. It also revealed a clear relationship between cluster radius and mass, as well as an interesting relation between effective radius and color that suggests varying structure across the clusters.

We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in relation to the Dickman function $\Psi(x,y)$. This provided a accurate estimate for certain ranges of $y$. By removing this restriction, our research aims to obtain an MPER-based formula for count of y-friable integers for a wide range of $y$. This formula allows $\Psi(x,y)$ to be applied to a wider range of $y$. Consequently, it from which relevant formula can be derived to count integers with limited prime factors (or B-rough integers). Notably, these formulas remain effective for y in the range $[1, x]$. This outcome is achieved even for values of $y$ significantly larger than $x$. This outcome has a direct impact on the Littlewood's Conjecture related to BAIA. It suggests that the BAIA is false for almost all real numbers.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't preserved when applying σ to X, indicating that defining topological entropy for free group currents F_N requires an injective mapping. Notably, one such injective morphism exists where the complexity functions have different linear growth rates, although they share the same topological entropy.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
Currently, language models (LMs) are often pre-trained on vast amounts of internet data and then fine-tuned for specific tasks.
Although this process is quite effective, LMs typically require significant fine-tuning when faced with new tasks, LMs' potential for unguided zero-shot transfer is limited, and cross-task generalization is a complex issue that needs to be addressed.
We propose using a single-user setting to study the generation of natural language by LMs, focusing on two key concerns: Can LMs successfully transfer what they have learned from one task to another without any additional training?
And can LMs be trained on a single task and then successfully trained on multiple other tasks without fine-tuning?
To investigate these issues, we introduce the Cross-task Generalization Evaluation (CAGE) framework, which consists of a comprehensive dataset and a comprehensive evaluation protocol to assess the capabilities of LMs in generating natural language in a wide range of scenarios, from zero-shot to multi-shot settings.
Our comprehensive evaluation of several popular LMs using the CAGE framework has provided valuable empirical findings that can guide future research on the development of LMs with enhanced cross-task generalization capabilities.

This research introduces m-ar-K-FastICA, an advanced version of the ar-K-FastICA
method. By integrating the ar-K-FastICA algorithm with the ar-Kernel method of
Feature Extraction, we developed an improved algorithm. Utilizing both second-order
statistics and non-linear ar-Kernel features of white noise assumption, m-ar-K-FastICA
enables efficient and fast computation of feature extracts with reduced complexity.
When applied to a variety of benchmark data sets, including the Yale Face Database, ORL
Face Database, CMU Pose Face Database, and the MIT Crabs Face Database, m-ar-K-FastICA
demonstrated superior performance in comparison to ar-K-FastICA. These results highlight
the method's effectiveness in feature extraction and classification tasks even in the
presence of random data.

This work offers an overview of requirements engineering in the gaming sector.
Existing research studies on this topic have been comprehensively examined.
Key characteristics of the gaming industry were identified and their connections to broader market dynamics discussed.
Additionally, unique aspects of virtual goods and customer behavior were briefly highlighted.
Finally, relevant requirements engineering methodologies and tools specifically tailored to gaming were harnessed to showcase potential applications and future research opportunities.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimally tuned hyperparameter that minimizes a performance measurement at a specific iteration, considering various performance measurement types. Two strategies are effectively employed to address this problem: finding the optimal parameter for an external optimizer and computing differential privacy bounds for the resulting solution. Notably, this paper successfully generalizes and applies these methods to previously solved problems, including finding the optimal learning rate in private stochastic gradient descent optimization, and determines the DPSGD performance bound for a specific cross-entropy model used in image classification.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly influence future cosmological research with its Visible and Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer instruments. The authors of this study analyzed how correlated readout noise affects in-flight measurements for the NISP detectors and proposed an analytical method for noise covariance matrices. Through experimental data analysis, a 1/f noise model was fitted for each NISP detector channel. The resulting noise levels range from approximately 0.3 to 2 times the readout noise squared (where the equivalent readout noise values are between 10 and 30 electrons). The authors found that the noise correlation lengths also vary between 40 and 90 equivalents of pixel, depending on the detector. These findings may have implications for the design of NISP's cool pixels and column readout modes.

We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the composition of 34,468 stars in our stellar chemical abundance database. This analysis allowed us to break down the patterns of seven key elemental ratios into distinct components, revealing similarities to both recent supernovae explosions and those occurring further in the past. By examining the behavior of these elements, we discovered that factors like distance from the galactic center and stellar velocity influence them. Additionally, we identified that elements formed in recent supernovae explosions vary with these influences, whereas elements formed in older explosions vary with stellar motion and galactic center distance less significantly. To understand this variation, we utilized the theory of how the galactic disk formed and evolved, which supported our findings and provided an explanation for the rate at which the supernovae explosion components changed. Furthermore, we found that the delayed components of certain elements could be used to estimate the age of the surrounding gas and that this could be used to set limits on the age of stellar populations.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 through social media and messaging apps, also fueling a surge in online rumors that hindered effective epidemic prevention and control. To better understand and address this issue, we developed a theoretical framework that views rumor dynamics as interconnected with emotional responses and information flows. Based on this theoretical basis, we designed and executed an online survey to collect real-world data, analyzing how emotions, information perception, and online behavior influence one another and promote the widespread dissemination of rumors. Our design-based analysis revealed that emotional reactions, information interpretation, and online interactions are deeply interconnected and reinforce each other, ultimately propelling the spread of rumors. To counter this effect, we proposed a policy designed to break the circular pattern in our model, validated by empirical data. Our design-based approach can aid in developing effective strategies to mitigate rumor dissemination on the internet.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on having an exhaustive understanding of their properties. Utilizing a large dataset from the PHOENIX survey, researchers have gathered exhaustive information on nearby galaxies' planetary nebulae using uniform processing methods and have been able to identify key parameters that significantly impact their structural formation, with key implications being used to enhance the accuracy of extragalactic distance measurements.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses and treatments. These analyses often involve complex computations and can take time, sometimes extending over days. To address this challenge, we introduce \emph{LifeStream}, a innovative solution capable of performing intricate analyses on large-scale physiological datasets in real-time and offline scenarios. Designing LifeStream was driven by multiple factors, including unique data characteristics, specific query patterns, and performance constraints, often overlooked in standard temporal database and streaming solutions. Moreover, we demonstrate through comprehensive evaluations that LifeStream substantially outperforms competing solutions for the intended workload, and our results have significant implications for designing efficient systems in data-intensive medical domains.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in a higher-dimensional space, do not fit the classification of a particular curve type. A new subset of curves, called time-like (1,3) Bertrand curves, is defined and identified based on the curves' curvature properties.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date. Given the lack of consensus on this issue, we view it as a problem suitable for solving using structured search methods, specifically Reversible Pointers. We focus on the task of classifying cats and dogs and demonstrate that reverse pointers can efficiently discover a highly competitive loss function, resulting in a neural network achieving greater than 90% accuracy with only 2.2 million gradient steps.
A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production, especially in polymer composites and filled materials widely used today. To simplify the problem and focus on essential physical mechanisms, our simplified model examines the linear elastic response and viscoflow of an unsaturated polymer. Although it neglects filler interactions, this research is currently applicable to various polymer systems and serves as a building block for more complex models in the future. By employing the Helix-Coil theory, we derive a dual-phase material model that captures both equilibrium properties and nonlinear crystallization dynamics driven by mechanical and thermal stimuli.

To analyze the impact of external pressure on a specific state of superconductivity within doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$, a novel method has been developed to isolate and study a bulk, chiral, superconducting state while minimizing influence from surface pairs, utilizing a unique device configuration that applies pressure solely from above. This method allows for a comparison with prior research on Bi$_2$Se$_3$ without such isolation. Doping with sodium and encapsulating between graphene layers facilitates this isolation. Experimental data shows that the superconducting transition temperature and the superconducting volume fraction both decrease as pressure is applied, indicating that the size of the superconducting volume fraction can be monitored precisely. Furthermore, surface-specific ARPES measurements with in-situ pressure reveal that the pressure does not significantly alter surface pairs but does alter the carrier density of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ due to its compressibility and that of graphene.

One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, we propose an alternative setting in which a single teacher can provide more flexible and quality feedback through a flexible feedback channel. We develop an algorithm called Flexible Feedback Teacher (F2T) that utilizes Bayesian Optimization to solve the problem. The results from our real-world experiments on laboratory robots demonstrate that F2T can produce superior results compared to other teacher algorithms and models.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the calculation of Euclidean distance between signal space points. Various structure implementations of equalizers have been investigated to enhance differential detection structure performance, yet existing methods often involve excessive computational cost, leading to performance degradation when channel disturbance occurs. A novel structure implementation of equalizer based on sliding window technique is proposed in this study. It leverages a second-order moving average filter to process differential phase data and efficiently process data using overlapping sliding windows. Simulations show that this proposed equalizer structure provides improved robustness against Doppler shift and channel disturbance, providing higher data integrity than existing structure implementations, with only marginal increase in computational cost.

New findings from 1D core-collapse simulations shed new light on the ultimate demise of massive stars, contradicting established parametric models. This study delves into the implications of these discoveries on the formation of colliding black-hole and neutron-star systems, as predicted by rigorous 3D simulations and gravitational wave observations. We adjust the traditional model of stellar collapse to reflect the latest insights, exploring its effects on the expected rate of mergers in the universe. Our analysis shows that the merger detection rate of black-hole and neutron-star systems could increase significantly, with a notable decline in systems comprising two neutron stars and a moderate rise in systems involving two black holes. In contrast, the merger detection rate of black-hole and neutron-star systems is relatively unaffected. To quantify these effects, we collaborate with the parameter estimation community, analyzing the parameters of merging systems that triggered the most profound reactions of gravitational waves so far. Our results show that the traditional model is unlikely responsible for any of these mergers, with some of them possibly involving the birth of a neutron star from the collapsing stellar core, or even a neutron star merging with another in some cases.

A previously reported finding from the research of the 1990s and 2000s is the strikingly uniform value of the ratio of variations to the mean in the energy density of quantum fields across various spacetime settings. Initially calculated using correlators of quantum field stress-energy tensors, the issue will now be re-examined using quantum thermodynamics. This is accomplished by determining the thermodynamic quantities known as heat capacity and compressibility directly from the value of quantum fields' energy density. The study focuses on scalar fields in the context of Drell-Horan high temperature scattering and Casimir effects, with particular attention given to the case of the 4-dimensional Schwarzschild black hole. The research demonstrates that the quantum fluctuations of the scalar field are in harmony with the observed findings of its classical counterpart, thus confirming the validity of the quantum stress-energy tensor operator approach used previously.

Current deep learning techniques for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically decreases when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they learn imperfect rain patterns from these artificial images.  Rain can in fact be viewed as a form of complex additive noise that adds complex transformations to the visible light.  Existing solutions often treat rain as simple noise and apply deconvolutional techniques to reverse this transformation.  A new proposal suggests using light scattering theory to model these complex transformations and treats rain removal as a multi-phase process: initially estimating the rain field from these estimates and then employing machine learning to unroll the deconvolutional process.  This approach reduces rain backscattering effects and enhances overall clarity.  Experimental results indicate that this method effectively handles difficult to penetrate rain and outperforms alternative solutions in this regard.  Code related to this research is available online at https://github.com/zhengqian99/LightScatteringDehinging.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness.
This study establishes conditions and proof of existence for a modified Branson-Howard equation under Navier boundary conditions on a bounded area of a high-dimensional space greater than two.

Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive set of questions aimed at assessing a person's personality, substance consumption habits, educational background, and demographic information. The dataset collected included responses from a diverse range of 2146 participants, who were asked to answer 12 questions related to drug abuse. The analysis revealed distinct patterns of substance consumption habits across different personality types and gender demographics. The data also showed that gender significantly influenced the likelihood of alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis consumption. Notably, alcohol and tobacco consumption aligned closely with the traditional impulsiveness scale, while a new, cross-gender scale of impulsiveness was developed to more accurately reflect these patterns. The study's approach can be applied to a diverse range of topics, including online surveys, telephone interviews, and face-to-face encounters.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.

Portfolio optimization is a complex process that necessitates resolving numerous linear and quadratic equations at its core. We suggest integrating the HHL and THCQD quantum algorithms into this complex process, specifically for stock portfolio optimization, and analyze their combined performance through a series of examples, including the DOW Jones components. Our research reveals that h cq l, an algorithm derived from this approach, can efficiently produce high-quality solutions with fewer iterations compared to its classical counterpart, QHCLO. Moreover, our findings indicate that the quantum portfolio optimization approach can yield exceptional results, such as maximizing portfolio returns while adhering to risk constraints.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are compatible. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both unpaired data and pair-wise data. By addressing these issues, the proposed method overcomes the problems and achieves significant improvements in ASR performance. Experiment results show that this approach results in a 2.20% reduction in word error rate compared to a baseline on the Librispeech dataset.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. Nonetheless, the optimal result can only be achieved within confined regions of space. Instead, the approach reveals relationships between key variables that can be utilized to identify optimal outcomes both internally and externally relative to these limited areas. Furthermore, specific properties are identified that can help visualize the complex structure of this geometric shape.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds for the convergence to equilibrium. Our main technique involves a coupling argument, drawing on the relationship between the uniform parking distribution and the cyclic lemma. This connects to prior studies by Bousquet-M\'elo, Picard, Rossin, and others.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage. A notable minimum in the critical voltage is found at a point corresponding to an increased resistance in the wire when in a superconducting state, which can be explained by the formation of a weak link due to a nanoscale normal region. The size of this region has a direct impact on the critical voltage, with both marquandite and perovskite phases of hydrogen niobate exhibiting different resistances that affect the critical voltage in distinct ways. Analyzing how the critical voltage changes with the extent of the anode oxide provides a means to differentiate between the two phases and locate any intermediate phases, which can be used to fabricate a multi-junction coherent quantum switch. The switch's operation is influenced by the extent of the normal regions in the wire, providing a robust foundation for the development of switch-based single flux quantum memory cells and switch-based quantum resonators.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially regarding its atmospheric features and mass. By applying advanced spectroscopic techniques, we obtained a basic analysis of GJ 229B and identified discrepancies in the dwarf's mass estimates across various models. These new data allowed us to estimate GJ 229B's mass and surface temperature, also revealing inconsistencies in the dwarf's age and host star's age. With the mass confirmed and temperature verified, we explored different evolutionary trajectories of GJ 229B. Depending on the dwarf's age and initial gas giant mass, various outcomes could occur such as a relatively young age, an unexpectedly old age with an unexpected gas giant mass, or a confirmed age of approximately 7.8 billion years with specific starting conditions.

Our study delves into the intricate relationship between the Bjorken scaling of structure functions and the emergence of a thermal medium. Specifically, we calculated the scaling violation of structure functions within a thermal medium using perturbation theory and DGLAP evolution, assuming the medium has a parton distribution. The condition necessary for Bjorken scaling of structure functions to occur is that the parton distribution must follow a power law with a coefficient greater than one. As part of this research, we apply the DGLAP equation to describe the evolution of structure functions in quark matter. The derived Bjorken sum rule is also verified through explicit calculations of structure functions in quark matter, which aligns with the outcome of the DGLAP evolution. The parton distribution density in quark matter follows a specific formula, which allows for a direct calculation of the structure functions, enabling us to derive the Bjorken sum rule, display the $Q^2$ dependence of structure functions, and determine a quark-matter analogue of the Glashow-Iliopoulos-Lewis sum rule.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

The Ω-baryon has long been a area of interest due to its content of sss quarks, which makes up the entire quark composition. Using the Light Front Quark Model, researchers have calculated various properties of the Ω-baryon, including its mass and form factors, considering a linear confining potential. The results obtained from this study show good agreement with available experimental data. Additionally, the form factor values derived from this study can be utilized in conjunction with other data to explore the decay process known as Ω-baryon decay.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses.

Building on cutting-edge experimental projects such as HIBEF at the XFEL, our calculations investigate the birefringent scattering of x-rays when interacting with two combined optical lasers, considering various possible outcomes. To aid in detecting quantum vacuum effects experimentally, our analysis focuses particularly on situations where x-ray photons show differences not just in polarization, but also in direction of propagation and potential energy changes.

This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space.

In our research, we explore the concept of unclonable encryption, both in quantum and classical settings, building upon the framework introduced by Bernstein and Raskin for measure-free cloning prevention. Our primary discovery is a unique quantum cloning-preventable encryption scheme, however, it comes with the limitation of an inefficient decryption process. We also introduce two additional efficient quantum encryption schemes with distinct properties, but, unlike the first scheme, their associated measurement functions are not linked to the encryption keys. Furthermore, we examine the feasibility of classical unclonable encryption and demonstrate that it's unattainable in the standalone setting. Notably, we identify a new class of classical protocols, defined by specific indistinguishability properties, that are clone-free despite being inherently classical.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the latter possessing unlimited transmission capabilities and
unlimited access to the transmitted message. It was demonstrated that modifying an
existing communication protocol can enable perfect secrecy through the use of a secret
key, regardless of the adversary's capabilities. Furthermore, an optimal protocol was
formulated and its capacity was defined. A comparison was also made with a scenario
where the adversary's knowledge was limited, with the question of whether reduced
key rates are sufficient in this context being explored.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged.
However, interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion splitting and additional
plasmon modes. By separating bands, we found that between specific energy
ranges, plasmons merged, and by increasing hole density, the plasmon frequency
could be lowered and plasmon damping reduced.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\lambda$. We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion.

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene on s-wave superconductors and magnetic layers on topological insulators. Recently, the spin-Orbit Proximity Effect was found to induce magnetic memory in the intrinsic intrinsic intrinsic Scandium Oxide (ScO2) by transferring Spin-Orbit Coupling from the Scandium Fluoride (ScF2) layer. In this study, we investigate the spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in ScO2/ScF2 bilayers and derive general formulas for calculating the modified Hamiltonian, including the exchange interaction, SOC, and the effective magnetic anisotropy. Our first-principles calculations yield estimates for various parameters, such as the exchange interaction, SOC strength, and the effective magnetic anisotropy. We also model the spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in ScO2/ScF2 bilayers and find that it can be attributed to the transfer of Spin-Orbit Coupling from ScF2 to ScO2.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples are also presented to illustrate the effectiveness of the approach.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on Basque data in comparison to their performance on English.
Our exploratory analysis of multiple architectures' performance on both languages
indicates that models tend to develop a general agreement pattern rather than
specifics to each language.
As a contribution to the field of NLP, we open the door to a new approach
that prioritizes the exploration of complex, hierarchical language structures
using low-resource data through machine learning.

HD80606b is a 2.7 times the mass of Jupiter planet that orbits a sun-like star in a highly eccentric path. As it approaches its star, the star's brightness increases substantially which causes substantial changes in the planet's heating in different areas. Based on a six-year observation, we used a robust model to create reliable estimates of the atmosphere's composition and properties over time. The results suggest that a thick cloud layer made of silicates covers the sub-stellar area when the planet is closest to its star, while the equatorial region experiences "clearing" due to cooling in this region. When the planet is furthest from its star, these clouds disappear and the atmosphere becomes transparent to heat. The atmosphere becomes transparent to heat when the planet is halfway through its orbit, which also marks the start of "thermal clearing" that lasts for half of its orbit. This study provides valuable insights into the atmosphere of HD80606b and could serve as a foundation for more complex future models taking orbit shape and temperature distribution into account.

Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation.  Nevertheless, currently available rehabilitation devices have limited force feedback options, which result in an incomplete range of interaction possibilities and restrict the design possibilities for force-based game mechanics.  This study aims to broaden these interaction possibilities and validation concepts for rehabilitation under controlled testing conditions.  To achieve this, we established a standardized force-based environment using a specialized game device that provides a broader range of force feedback options.  This environment was paired with a standard methodology (TUG) that evaluates participants' perception of game mechanics and rehabilitation effort.  To test our concept, we ran three distinct gameplay scenarios and collected data to analyze participants' responses and validate the MUG concept through statistical modeling.  Our findings revealed that specific force feedback game mechanics can be effectively achieved and that users associate increased game difficulty with higher physical effort, which paves the way for tailoring interaction concepts to individual rehabilitation needs.

Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their use in certain sensitive groups. Therefore, biologically modeled "digital patients" have been proposed for acquiring imaging data for research and image analysis purposes. Nonetheless, existing methods for simulating positron emission tomography scans do not accurately model the physics of the detectors nor do they consider different radiotracer types. In this paper, we present a novel method for simulating four different radiotracers for brain positron emission tomography scans, that also realistically models the scanner's detection processes. Our method can also be applied to other radiotracers and scanners. Our results show that the developed model accurately radiologically behaves, with a low error rate of 4.6 percent when compared to actual data acquired with a real scanner.
